title: Basic Computer Literacy and Use of Software Packages

lessons.title: Computer basics for the abattoir supervisor
lessons.html:
Why supervisors need computer skills

More and more abattoir records are kept on computers: slaughter registers, weighing and classification data, temperature logs, time and attendance, stock and reports. A supervisor who can use a computer works faster, makes fewer mistakes and can find information quickly.

Parts of a computer system

PartWhat it does
Monitor (screen)Shows information
Keyboard and mouseUsed to type and to point and click
Computer (desktop or laptop)Processes and stores information
PrinterPrints reports and labels
Network and internetConnects computers so they can share information and send e-mail
StorageHard drive, USB flash drive or cloud storage where files are saved

Hardware and software

Hardware is the physical equipment you can touch. Software is the programs that run on it. The operating system (for example Windows) manages the computer. Application programs do specific jobs: a word processor for letters and reports, a spreadsheet for numbers and tables, e-mail for messages, and abattoir software for weighing and records.

Starting and shutting down

  • Switch on and log in with your own username and password.
  • Save your work often.
  • Close programs and log off or shut down properly at the end of the day. Do not just switch off the power.

Files and folders

Work is saved as files (for example a report). Files are kept in folders, like papers in a filing cabinet. Use clear names, such as Slaughter report 2026-10-18, so anyone can find the file later.

lessons.title: Word processing, spreadsheets and e-mail
lessons.html:
Word processing

A word processor (such as Microsoft Word) is used for letters, memos, procedures and reports.

  • Type the text, then use bold, headings and bullet lists to make it easy to read.
  • Use spell check, but read the document yourself as well.
  • Use tables for information like a duty roster.
  • Save the file before printing.

Spreadsheets

A spreadsheet (such as Microsoft Excel) arranges information in rows and columns. Each box is a cell, named by its column letter and row number, for example B3. Spreadsheets are ideal for slaughter numbers, overtime hours and temperature readings.

Simple formulas

A formula starts with an equals sign:

  • =B2+B3 adds two cells.
  • =SUM(B2:B8) adds a range of cells, for example a week's slaughter numbers.
  • =AVERAGE(C2:C8) gives the average.
  • =B2/C2*100 could calculate a dressing percentage if B2 is carcass mass and C2 is live mass.

Check formulas with a calculator the first time to make sure they are correct.

E-mail

  • Use a clear subject line, such as Chiller 3 temperature problem, Tuesday.
  • Keep the message short and polite.
  • Check you are sending to the right people before you click send.
  • Attach files when needed and check the attachment is the right one.
  • Do not forward confidential information to people who do not need it.

lessons.title: Using abattoir software safely
lessons.html:
Abattoir systems

Many abattoirs use software linked to scales and label printers. When a carcass is weighed, the system records the carcass number, owner, mass and classification and prints a label. Data entered wrongly can send a carcass to the wrong owner or customer, so accuracy is important.

Good data entry

  • Check the lot or owner number before the first carcass of each lot.
  • Look at the screen after each entry to confirm it is correct.
  • If you make a mistake, correct it immediately using the correct procedure and tell the supervisor; do not delete records without authority.
  • Report system faults straight away and use the backup paper procedure if the system is down.

Security

  • Use your own password and never share it. The system records who entered or changed data.
  • Choose a strong password with letters, numbers and symbols. Do not write it on the screen.
  • Lock the computer when you walk away.
  • Do not open e-mail attachments or links from people you do not know; they may contain viruses.
  • Do not plug unknown USB drives into work computers.
  • Do not install programs without permission from IT.

Backups

Important files must be backed up so they are not lost if the computer fails or is stolen. Ask IT or your manager where files should be saved so they are included in backups.

Health and safety at the computer

Sit with your back supported, the screen at eye level and your wrists straight. Take short breaks to rest your eyes. Keep liquids away from keyboards. In wet production areas, use only computers and screens designed for those conditions.

Key points

  • Hardware is the equipment; software is the programs.
  • Use clear file names and save work often.
  • Spreadsheet formulas start with an equals sign, for example =SUM(B2:B8).
  • Check data entries in abattoir software; errors affect traceability.
  • Never share passwords and lock the computer when you leave it.
